summary: Extends the LDP and IGP synchronization mechanism of RFC 5443 to broadcast links with more than one LDP peer, where metric increase only applies to the link as a whole. It updates RFC 5443 and is informational.

eli5.summary: When a new neighbor joins a shared link, traffic should not go there until it is ready. This fixes how to wait for each neighbor.

questions: what is a cut-edge in ospf
how does ldp igp sync work on broadcast networks
subtitle: How a router can bring up a shared LAN link without black-holing traffic while LDP catches up.

tldr.problem: RFC 5443 raises a link's metric until LDP is ready, but on a broadcast network a router advertises one cost for the whole network, not one per peer. Raising it hurts traffic through peers that were already working.
tldr.mechanism: The router whose link is coming up simply leaves that link out of its link-state advertisement until LDP is operational with all peers on it, unless the interface is a cut-edge. No protocol messages change.
tldr.outcome: Traffic is not sent toward a neighbor that has no LDP label paths yet, and the other routers on the network do nothing. It updates RFC 5443 and is Informational.

today: RFC 6138 is Informational and, per the metadata, is not obsoleted or updated by a later RFC. It updates RFC 5443.

sections.title: LDP IGP Synchronization Recap
sections.content:
In RFC 5443, when LDP is not fully operational on a link, the IGP advertises the link with maximum cost. That keeps transit traffic off the link if possible. Once LDP is operational, meaning all label bindings have been exchanged, the link is advertised with its correct cost.

The aim is that an LDP label switch path (LSP) exists all along the IGP shortest path. This RFC explains why the approach breaks on broadcast links and defines a fix.
sections.eli5: A road should only be opened to cars once the road signs are up. Otherwise drivers get lost.

sections.title: Why Broadcast Networks Are a Problem
sections.content:
On a broadcast network, a router's Link State Advertisement (LSA) holds a single cost to the network, not a separate cost to each peer. The RFC walks through a topology with routers A, B, C and E on one broadcast network, where B's link comes up.

In the first interpretation, every attached router advertises maximum cost. Traffic may be diverted onto the link that just came up and black-holed until LDP is operational. Route churn also sends unaffected traffic, such as PE1 to PE3, over a sub-optimal path. Reverting the cost also needs coordination between all the routers.

In the second interpretation, only B advertises a high cost. But A's cost to reach B is not high, so A-B-PE2 becomes the shortest path before LDP peering A-B is operational. VPN traffic from PE1 to PE2 is dropped at A.
sections.eli5: If everyone yells that the road is closed, cars wander onto the wrong streets. If only the new road says it, the old road's drivers still turn into it too early.

sections.title: The Solution: Hold Back the Link
sections.content:
The root cause is that the link-state database does not show the new link as high cost in both directions. A broadcast network is advertised as a pseudonode, and the cost from the pseudonode to each router is zero in SPF.

The fix is to keep the coming-up link out of the database unless absolutely necessary. Only the router whose link is coming up does anything. The IGP and LDP adjacency bring-up procedures are unchanged.

When the router's first adjacency to the broadcast network is about to be reflected in its LSA, it checks whether the interface is a cut-edge. If not, the update that adds the link to the pseudonode is postponed until LDP is operational with all the LDP peers on that interface, and then the LSA is updated and flooded. If it is a cut-edge, the update MUST NOT be delayed by LDP.

  • OSPF: the Router-LSA is not given a Link Type 2 (link to transit network) entry for the subnet until then.
  • IS-IS: the Link State PDU gets an IS Reachability TLV (or Extended IS Reachability TLV) to the pseudonode only after that.

The solution can be introduced gradually without backward compatibility issues.
sections.eli5: The new kid does not announce they are in the room until they have their books. The only exception is if they are the only way to reach the next room.

sections.title: Detecting a Cut-Edge
sections.content:
A directly connected network with no alternate path to reach it makes its interface a cut-edge for that router. If it goes down, the network splits into two disjoint sub-graphs. Delaying the link in that case would only isolate the neighbor, so the delay is skipped.

Appendix A says the router can find this during an intra-area SPF run or from the previous run. A pending SPF MUST be executed first. Detection should not need extra SPF runs or raise the complexity of SPF.
sections.eli5: If a bridge is the only way to a village, you cannot keep it closed while you wait. If there is another road, you can.

sections.title: Scope and Applicability
sections.content:
The document does not define how to tell that LDP is operational with a neighbor. At publication, LDP End-of-LIB (RFC 5919) seemed the preferred method. LDP not being configured on some routers or interfaces is out of scope.

The method extends easily to point-to-point links, and the older RFC 5443 method can still be used on those links, so both can coexist. As an optional benefit, left for further study, it can give synchronization when one end of an adjacency supports no sync method at all. For broadcast networks that is not straightforward.
sections.eli5: The rule works for shared rooms and for private hallways. It does not say how to check someone is ready, only that you should wait for it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
No new considerations beyond RFC 5443. The RFC notes that a high metric can push traffic onto an alternate path with so many hops that the end-to-end path exceeds 255 hops and becomes unreachable, which could be exploited if an attacker controls metrics.

The same problem exists in a plain IP network with a link-state IGP, so operators need to apply policy and security to how link metrics are determined and distributed.
sections.eli5: If a bad person can change the road-length signs, they can send drivers on very long trips. Guard the signs.
